A politician is a person who is actively involved in politics — that is, someone who seeks, holds, or works toward a position of power in government, or who makes it their career to shape how a country, state, or city is governed.

A politician is someone whose main job revolves around getting into government and making decisions that affect society.

A politician's work typically involves several things:

Getting elected. Most politicians don't just walk into power — they campaign. They give speeches, meet voters, make promises, run advertisements, and try to persuade people to vote for them. This process is called running for office or contesting an election.

Representing people. Once elected, a politician is supposed to represent the people who voted for them (called their constituents). This means listening to their concerns, speaking up for them in government, and making decisions in their interest — at least in theory.

Making laws and policies. Politicians debate issues in parliaments, congresses, or councils, and vote on new laws and rules. They decide things like how much tax people pay, how schools are funded, how roads are built, and how the country handles crime, healthcare, or foreign relations.

Negotiating and building alliances. Politics involves a lot of deal-making. Politicians need to work with other politicians — sometimes from opposing parties — to get things done. This requires persuasion, compromise, and sometimes strategy.

Politicians operate at many levels of government:

Local level — These are politicians who govern cities, towns, or districts. Examples include mayors, city council members, and municipal commissioners. They handle issues like local roads, water supply, garbage collection, and local schools.

State or regional level — These politicians govern a state, province, or region within a country. Examples include state governors, chief ministers, and state legislators. They handle matters like state law, regional infrastructure, and state budgets.

National level — These are the most prominent politicians, governing an entire country. Examples include presidents, prime ministers, senators, members of parliament (MPs), and cabinet ministers. They shape the country's laws, foreign policy, military decisions, and national economy.
The Two Sides of the Word: Its Connotations

This is one of the most interesting things about the word "politician" — it can carry very different feelings depending on context.

Used neutrally, it simply describes someone's profession, the same way you'd call someone a doctor or an engineer. "She became a politician at age 35." No judgment is attached — it just means she entered the world of politics.

Used positively, it can suggest someone skilled, experienced, and effective at navigating the complex world of government. "He's a brilliant politician — he knows how to get things done." Here, being a "good politician" means being someone who understands the system, builds coalitions, and achieves results for their people.

Used negatively, and this is very common in everyday speech, the word suggests someone who is more interested in gaining power, winning elections, and saying whatever people want to hear, rather than genuinely serving the public. "Don't believe him — he's just a politician." This use implies dishonesty, self-interest, or empty promises. Phrases like "typical politician" or "just playing politics" carry this cynical flavor.

So the word is not inherently good or bad — context and tone tell you which meaning is intended.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are examples showing the range of use:

  • "The veteran politician had served in parliament for over three decades." — neutral, describing someone experienced in politics.
  • "She is a talented politician who genuinely cares about the people she represents." — positive, suggesting skill and good intentions.
  • "He gave a vague answer — very much like a politician avoiding the real question." — negative, suggesting evasiveness and insincerity.
  • "Young politicians today face immense pressure from social media." — neutral, referring to people in the political profession generally.
  • "The politician promised lower taxes right before the election but never delivered." — negative, implying strategic dishonesty.

Understanding a word fully also means knowing what it is not. Here are a few words people sometimes confuse with "politician":

Statesman / Stateswoman — This is a more respectful, elevated version of a politician. A statesman is someone who is widely admired for wisdom, integrity, and putting the nation's long-term good above personal gain. Not every politician earns this label — it's considered a higher compliment. All statesmen are politicians, but not all politicians are statesmen.

Civil servant / Bureaucrat — These are government employees who do the daily administrative work of running a government — processing files, implementing policies, running departments. They are not politicians because they are not elected and do not seek power through elections. They work under politicians.

Activist — An activist is someone who campaigns for a cause (like environmental protection or human rights) but does not necessarily hold or seek government office. Activists push politicians from the outside; politicians govern from the inside.

Diplomat — A diplomat represents their country in dealings with foreign governments. They work in embassies and negotiate international agreements. While they are part of the political world, they are not elected and their role is specifically about international relations, not domestic lawmaking.
The Broader Idea Behind the Word

A politician is someone who has chosen to engage with one of humanity's oldest and most complex activities: organizing large groups of people, managing shared resources, and making decisions that affect the lives of many. It's a role that requires communication skills, strategic thinking, the ability to handle public scrutiny, and — ideally — genuine concern for the public good.

The word carries a slight tension built into it: politicians need to win elections to serve, which means they need to be popular; but truly serving the public sometimes requires making unpopular decisions. This tension between what's politically useful and what's genuinely good is exactly why the word often carries a skeptical or critical undertone in everyday conversation.

When someone says "they're being a politician about it," they mean the person is dodging, spinning, or calculating their words for advantage — rather than just being honest and direct.

A politician is a person who seeks or holds power in government through elections or appointments, whose job involves making laws, representing people, and shaping public policy — and who, depending on how they conduct themselves, may be seen as a dedicated public servant or as a self-interested operator playing the system for personal gain.
